articles.title: Built in 1584 and abandoned in the 18th century, a roofless Scottish castle with original fireplaces and staircases is on sale for £120,000
articles.summary: A roofless Scottish castle that has stood for centuries is back on the market for offers over £120,000.
articles.body: A roofless Scottish castle that has stood for centuries is back on the market for offers over £120,000. Baltersan Castle, near Maybole in Ayrshire, was built in 1584 and deserted around the middle of the 18th century. Despite its long period without a roof, much of the Category A-listed building remains intact, including original fireplaces, staircases, floor levels and window openings.The castle occupies 0.75 acres of land, around 10 miles from Ayr and 45 miles from Glasgow. Architect and designer Charles Rennie Mackintosh sketched the building in 1895, while poets Robert Burns and John Keats also visited it. According to The Scottish Sun, the property is being marketed as a rare restoration opportunity.Baltersan Castle: The 16th-century Scottish tower house on saleBaltersan Castle is being offered for offers over £120,000, a price lower than many flats in Edinburgh and Glasgow. The property is a roofless, Category A-listed building near Maybole in Ayrshire. It comes with 0.75 acres of land and lies around 10 miles from Ayr and 45 miles from Glasgow. Selling agent Galbraith described it as an “exceptional” L-plan tower house with “national architectural and historic significance”.The agent also called the sale a “unique opportunity” to buy and restore one of the region’s most important historic buildings. However, planning consent for rebuilding and converting the tower house has expired.Baltersan Castle was constructed in 1584 by John Kennedy of Pennyglen and his wife, Margaret Cathcart. The Kennedys were a distinguished family in the Carrick area. The building is described as an L-plan tower house, and the agent describes it as a building of “national architectural and historic significance.” The structure was deserted around the middle of the 18th century. Despite that long period of abandonment, much of the building remains intact, including its original architectural details.A roofless structure still preserves centuries-old architectural detailsAlthough Baltersan Castle has stood without a roof for centuries, much of its original structure remains intact. The Category A-listed building retains its original fireplaces and staircases, along with its floor levels, roof geometry and window openings.The property also comes with 0.75 acres of land. According to the selling agent, the castle has retained a “remarkable degree” of structural integrity despite its long period of abandonment.Poets and a designer are among the notable figures linked to the castleBaltersan Castle attracted the attention of architect and designer Charles Rennie Mackintosh, who sketched the building in 1895 while holidaying in the area. The castle was also visited by poets Robert Burns and John Keats.In 2024, it emerged that the castle was in line for a £2 million restoration. It had previously been purchased by Italian computer engineer Angelo Ovidi for an undisclosed fee, with plans to restore the structure. The property is now back on the market, but planning consent for rebuilding and conversion has expired.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information. articles.title: In 1864, Abraham Lincoln donated a signed photograph to help Union soldiers' families; generations later, it surfaced in an old desk with a forgotten newspaper clipping and sold for $149,020 at auction
articles.summary: Some historical treasures spend decades behind glass, carefully catalogued and admired.
articles.body: Some historical treasures spend decades behind glass, carefully catalogued and admired. Others wait quietly in forgotten corners of family homes, their significance hidden until an unexpected discovery brings the past back to life. A signed photograph of Abraham Lincoln followed the latter path, surviving for generations in a Massachusetts family before emerging with an old newspaper clipping that helped establish its remarkable history. The portrait eventually sold at auction for $149,020, states an auction report by RR Auction.A photograph with a wartime purposeAccording to the auction report, the photograph, known as Lincoln's Penny Profile, captures the 16th US president in a right-facing profile. Measuring 2.25 by 4 inches, the carte-de-visite portrait was taken on February 9, 1864, by Anthony Berger at Mathew Brady's photographic studio in Washington.The image became one of Lincoln's most recognisable likenesses and later served as the principal photographic reference for Victor David Brenner's design of the Lincoln cent. The same photographic sitting also produced the portrait that would eventually be adapted for the five-dollar bill.This particular example carries an additional distinction: Lincoln's signature appears in ink at the bottom, while an inscription on the reverse records its original purpose, adds the description of the portrait.Supporting Union soldiers' familiesAs per the report, in December 1864, as the American Civil War continued, Lincoln contributed six signed photographic portraits to the Soldiers' Aid Society of Westford, Massachusetts. The photographs were intended for sale at a fundraising event held on December 14, with proceeds supporting the families of local Union soldiers.Unable to provide federal funds directly to the organisation, Lincoln offered something of personal and historical value instead. The signed portraits became part of an effort to raise money for those bearing the cost of the war at home.The inscription on the reverse of the photograph confirms its connection to the Westford benefit, making it more than a presidential portrait. It is a surviving record of a wartime charitable initiative, adds the online report.A forgotten clipping reveals its historyAs per the description, the photograph is believed to have been acquired at the fundraising event by Charles G. Sargent, a prominent Westford industrialist and civic leader. It subsequently passed to his son, Allan C. Sargent, who was known for his preservation work and involvement in historical organisations.The portrait remained within the family for roughly a century before its significance was brought back into focus. An accompanying newspaper clipping from 1924 documented Lincoln's donation of the six photographs and affirmed the authenticity of his signature, adds the report.The clipping was discovered at the back of an old frame when the photograph resurfaced in a desk, providing a valuable link between the object and its original purpose.A rare piece of American historyThe photograph, presented in very good to fine condition with minor signs of age, was authenticated by PSA/DNA and accompanied by documentation detailing its provenance. Its eventual sale for $149,020 reflects the appeal of an object that combines presidential history, photographic significance and a documented connection to Civil War-era philanthropy.Images Courtesy: RR AuctionYou use AI every day. articles.title: Army to unveil new land warfare doctrine: What may change and why it matters
articles.summary: The army is about to get a new land warfare doctrine.
articles.body: The army is about to get a new land warfare doctrine. Defence minister Rajnath Singh will release it on Friday, the third and final day of the biannual Army Commanders' Conference, the first under General Dhiraj Seth as Army chief. The three-day meeting brings together the commanders-in-chief of the army's six operational and one training command and the principal staff officers at Army Headquarters. The defence ministry says the doctrine will give the force an overarching framework for the changing character of war, at a time when drones, precision strikes and networked operations are deciding more and more battles.The last land warfare doctrine was released in December 2018, about a year and a half after the joint doctrine of the armed forces of April 2017. Earlier editions came out in 1998 and 2004. The 2018 document dealt with the geostrategic environment, the spectrum of conflict, hybrid warfare, multi-front capability, surveillance, precision strike, information warfare, space warfare and special forces, and it was meant to form the basis for strategies on the northern and western fronts. The new version is expected to cover how operations are integrated across the conventional domains and newer ones such as cyber, space and electronic warfare, and the growing use of unmanned platforms and artificial intelligence in surveillance, targeting and decision-making.A good deal has happened since 2018. The army has been through a long stand-off with China along the Line of Actual Control. In May 2025, Operation Sindoor showed what long-range precision fire against targets across the border looks like. On May 7, India announced strikes on nine terrorist infrastructure sites in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir and the army took on seven of them, using artillery and precision-guided munitions, including loitering munitions. At the same time, the wars in Ukraine and West Asia have brought drones, loitering munitions, ballistic and cruise missiles, electronic warfare and integrated air defence to the fore. Counter-insurgency operations in Jammu and Kashmir and the north-east have carried on throughout.The doctrine will be read against two fronts. In the north, the stand-off with China has made rapid mobilisation, high-altitude logistics and round-the-clock surveillance a priority. In the west, the Army has to deal with conventional formations, drones, missiles and cross-border attacks.The lessons from Ukraine and West Asia are also expected to feature. Drones and loitering munitions now handle reconnaissance, target acquisition and attack, while electronic warfare can knock out communications, navigation and command networks. With constant surveillance overhead, troops and vehicles find it harder to move unseen, which makes camouflage, deception, dispersal and mobility matter more. Ballistic and cruise missiles can hit headquarters, airfields, ammunition depots and supply points far behind the front line, so the Army has to think about how to protect them and how to keep communications going when networks are jammed or damaged. Artificial intelligence and digital command systems can speed up the way information is processed and shared, but they need reliable data, secure networks and trained people to work.The Integrated Defence Services issued its Joint Doctrine for Multi-Domain Operations in August 2025, a framework for bringing together land, air, maritime, space, cyber and information capabilities. For the army, that could mean combining satellite imagery, drone feeds, electronic intelligence, artillery targeting and air support to find and engage an enemy. The test is whether the right information reaches the right commander quickly, and whether the three services can work together when an adversary goes after communications, navigation or surveillance systems before attacking.The Army is also changing its own structure, and that may show up in the new document. Integrated Battle Groups bring combat and support elements under one commander for faster mobilisation. Bhairav battalions are light, mobile forces for reconnaissance and rapid response. Shaktibaan regiments and Divyastra batteries add drones, loitering munitions and precision strike, and Ashni platoons give infantry battalions their own drone capability.

articles.title: CM Devendra Fadnavis announces mega chemical park near Vadhvan Port, seeks Centre’s nod for 2,500-5,000 acres in Maharashtra
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis has announced plans for a mega chemical park near Vadhvan Port and urged the Centre to approve the
articles.body: MUMBAI: Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis has announced plans for a mega chemical park near Vadhvan Port and urged the Centre to approve the project, for which the state government is willing to allot between 2,500 and 5,000 acres.Speaking at the inauguration of Indochem in Goregaon, Fadnavis said the state government would make the land available for the proposed park and asked the Centre to sanction the project.The proposed location is significant as Dahanu taluka in Palghar district was previously designated an ecologically sensitive zone.Union minister for chemicals and fertilisers JP Nadda said the Centre had already announced the Bhavya Rasayan scheme in the Union Budget. Under the scheme, the Centre will provide Rs 1,000 crore, while the state government will contribute Rs 500 crore.Nadda said the Centre would facilitate environmental clearances for the scheme.The proposed initiative is part of the Centre’s Viksit Bharat vision and its goal of building a $1 trillion economy by 2040.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: In 2000, Durham repairman Gene Dillard began filling his yard with metal art; 15 years later, he started a mosaic home with hand tools, and neighbors gave tours
articles.summary: Discover the fascinating story of Gene Dillard, a former repairman who transformed his home into a stunning mosaic art piece in Durham, North Carolina. Uncover the creativity, inspiration, and community interactions behind this unique project.
articles.body: Most people who spend their working lives repairing other people’s equipment do not expect to spend retirement building an elaborate work of folk art. Perhaps a veggie patch in the back or a fishing pole. Few grab a pair of tile nippers and a bucket of shattered mirrors. On Elgin Street in Durham, North Carolina, Gene Dillard began filling his yard with metal sculptures around 2000 and started covering his house with mosaics around 2015, according to a PBS North Carolina profile. Dillard says he had never made art before taking on the project and had spent his working life as a repairman. The SPACES archives document the home’s mirror-covered exterior, backyard spaceship, pottery fence, and yard sculptures. None of it was meant as a business. Dillard says he doesn't sell his art and has manufactured most of it with modest hand tools.From repair work to mosaic artDillard was a repairman by trade and spent a good part of his working life maintaining scientific and restaurant supplies, according to Indy Week. He moved from San Diego to North Carolina in the 1980s and settled in Durham’s Northgate Park district. He tells us that he moved into the Elgin Street residence about the year 2000 and that is when the garden began to transform.The first were metallic. Dillard made a sea monster out of rebar that holds his mailbox, a surfer riding a wave down the front lawn, and a rainbow mermaid observing from the right. He has remarked that a first major mosaic, done together with a friend, got under his skin and he has been hooked on the craft ever since. He also said he likes the repetitive motion of the job, which helps explain why the project never ceased.Mirrors, pottery, and a spaceship in the backyardIn 2015, Dillard grew tired of making yard sculptures and began covering his house and garage with mosaics. He covered the walls of the front and driveway with pieces of mirror, first in winding vines that soon sprung from the wall in three-dimensional chunks. By 2017 he’d finished three walls of the home, three of the garage, and it was all cut with handheld tile nippers.In the backyard, Dillard built a spaceship from two-inch-square metal tubes welded together and wrapped in rebar. Green, blue and amber bottles cover the structure, filtering colored light into its interior at different times of day. Around it, a fence he completed over three years during the COVID quarantine holds pottery donated by friends and guests. Many works are presented with the potter’s name facing outward, a reference to craftspeople whose signatures are often unseen. Seven faces, including a Cyclops, a King, a Queen and a Knight, are made of rebar and cement and studded with shards, bottles and one unopened bottle of Jack Daniels. Within, each large window has its own mosaic valance, doors are trimmed in a matching daisy pattern, and the entryway over the front door has been converted to a double-height opening. Online maps label the address as Gene Dillard’s Fantasy Land.Dillard has been forthright about the source of the urge. He cited a few self-taught craftsmen as his influence in a 2017 interview with the Strange Carolinas travel site, including Minnie Evans, whose drawings he adores, and Henry Warren, whose small village in Prospect Hill he dubbed his personal Mecca. Warren’s Shangri-La is a town of 27 stone structures, which the retired tobacco farmer created on his own, commencing in 1968, the state tourism portal VisitNC says.Calling on a private residenceDillard says his neighbors have been supportive. In a PBS North Carolina feature about the house, one individual interviewed stated visitors sometimes feel overwhelmed by it and others are reluctant to come up the driveway, so they wanted a handout that points out minor details people might otherwise miss.SPACES describes the front and back yards as open to the public at all hours and claims Dillard is pleased to chat with guests if he happens to be there during the day. The inside of the house is his living space, and it is still a private property on a residential street, so a quiet visit and pleasant wave go a long way. The house is at 2706 Elgin St., in Northgate Park.And this is just the beginning. In winter 2024, the mosaic face of the chimney fell off, and Dillard wants to create a replacement. He's also got a wizard sculpture coming up that will have a lamp to light up his yard at night. The mosaic-covered exterior remains an evolving work of folk art, visible to passersby while the house itself remains a private residence.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2014, Sofía Vergara bought a Beverly Hills villa for $10.6 million; after renovating it and asking $19.6 million in 2022, the 11,000-square-foot estate finally sold for $13.7 million after nearly two years
articles.summary: Hollywood actor Sofía Vergara sold her Tuscan-style Beverly Hills estate for $13.7 million after nearly two years on the market.
articles.body: Hollywood actor Sofía Vergara sold her Tuscan-style Beverly Hills estate for $13.7 million after nearly two years on the market. Vergara bought the property for $10.6 million in 2014, renovated it with her then-husband Joe Manganiello, and initially listed it for $19.6 million in July 2022. As reported by Architectural Digest, the sale was reported on April 25, 2024, after the couple had reduced the asking price several times. The final price was nearly $6 million below the original listing price, but $3.1 million above the amount Vergara had paid for the home in 2014. The estate covers around 11,000 square feet and has seven bedrooms and 11 bathrooms. It sits on a plot of just over half an acre, behind gates and tall hedges.A $19.6 million asking price that kept fallingWhen Vergara and Manganiello put the property on the market in July 2022, they asked $19.6 million for it. In a 2022 report by the Los Angeles Times, the price was nearly double the $10.6 million paid for the property in 2014. The couple had already moved to a larger home in the Beverly Park neighbourhood in 2020. The new listing offered more than 11,000 square feet of living space, with a gym, movie theatre, wine cellar and wet bar. After the house remained unsold for about a year, the asking price was reduced to $17.99 million in the summer of 2023, according to Architectural Digest. It was subsequently listed again in early 2024 for around $13.9 million. The property eventually sold for $13.7 million.Inside the Tuscan-style estateThe home was built in 2006 and has a design inspired by Tuscan villas. As reported by the Los Angeles Times, the interior features neutral colours in the main living areas, while black accents appear in the office, theatre and bar. A spiral staircase connects the two levels, and the entrance has a rotunda-topped foyer. The formal living room features a large stone fireplace. The kitchen has a central island and dual sinks, while French doors connect the main living areas to the garden.The backyard includes a swimming pool, spa, several patios and a covered outdoor sitting area. Tall hedges and lawns provide privacy around the property. As reported by Architectural Digest, all seven bedrooms have en-suite bathrooms. The primary bedroom also has an outdoor patio with a stone fireplace and seating. Other features include a wet bar, a wine cellar that can hold 3,000 bottles, a wine-tasting room, a gym and a large home theatre with dark-wood detailing.Renovations before the saleVergara and Manganiello worked with Los Angeles designer Jennifer Bevan to remodel the home. In a July 2022 report, Architectural Digest described the renovation as a complete redesign, highlighting the high ceilings, dark-wood details and statement chandeliers. The couple’s decision to sell followed their move to a larger Beverly Park property. According to Architectural Digest, the 17,000-square-foot home had undergone two years of renovation before it was ready for them to move in. The Beverly Hills estate was therefore no longer their main home when they began trying to sell it.What the final sale price meansThe $13.7 million sale price was $5.9 million below the original $19.6 million asking price. However, compared with the $10.6 million purchase price in 2014, the sale represented a difference of $3.1 million before accounting for renovation costs, taxes, transaction fees and other expenses. The final figure was also slightly below the last reported asking price of $13.9 million. Vergara, best known for playing Gloria Delgado-Pritchett in the television comedy ‘Modern Family,’ was also serving as a judge on America’s Got Talent at the time of the 2022 listing, according to the Los Angeles Times. After nearly two years of attempted sale, the Beverly Hills villa finally changed hands in April 2024 for $13.7 million.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Rival factions, civil war & shadow of terror: Why Libya is still broken 15 years after Gaddafi's bloody end
articles.summary: Muammar Gaddafi's 42-year rule over Libya ended violently near his hometown of Sirte on October 20, 2011, when opposition fighters captured and killed him.
articles.body: Muammar Gaddafi's 42-year rule over Libya ended violently near his hometown of Sirte on October 20, 2011, when opposition fighters captured and killed him.His death marked the culmination of an uprising that began months earlier and was bolstered by a Nato-led military intervention. But the fall of one of Africa's longest-serving rulers did not bring the oil-rich North African country the stability many Libyans had hoped for.Fifteen years later, Libya remains divided between rival political administrations and competing centres of military power. Although a unified national budget was approved in April 2026 and a United Nations-backed agreement in August set out steps towards long-delayed elections, the country continues to struggle with political fragmentation, armed groups and disputes over state resources.The question, therefore, is not just how Gaddafi fell, but why his removal failed to bring stability to Libya.Why Gaddafi's regime fellThe uprising against Muammar Gaddafi began in February 2011, amid the Arab Spring protests that had toppled long-serving rulers in Tunisia and Egypt.Protests erupted in Benghazi on February 15, following the arrest of government critics, including a lawyer representing families of prisoners killed in the 1996 Abu Salim prison massacre. Libyan security forces responded with tear gas, batons and violence against demonstrators.The crackdown escalated the protests into an armed rebellion, with opposition forces taking control of parts of eastern Libya. On February 26, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 1970, imposing sanctions and referring the situation to the International Criminal Court.On March 17, it adopted Resolution 1973, authorising member states to take “all necessary measures” to protect civilians. Nato took command of the military operation on March 31, enforcing an arms embargo and no-fly zone and conducting military operations.Tripoli fell to opposition forces on August 21, 2011, forcing Gaddafi's regime out of the capital. Two months later, as rebels overran his hometown of Sirte, Gaddafi attempted to flee in a convoy that came under Nato air strikes.He was captured alive by fighters from Misrata on October 20 and killed shortly afterwards. A subsequent Human Rights Watch investigation found evidence that he had been beaten and wounded after his capture, raising questions over a possible extrajudicial killing.What happened to Libya after Gaddafi's deathGaddafi's death in October 2011 left Libya facing the challenge of building a new political system while armed groups that had fought his regime retained their weapons and influence.The National Transitional Council oversaw the transition before handing power to an elected General National Congress in August 2012. However, successive governments struggled to bring militias under state control, while political divisions and insecurity continued to deepen.Libya's civil war deepens the divideLibya descended into a full-scale civil war in 2014, as political divisions and rival armed groups fractured the country.In May that year, military commander Khalifa Haftar launched Operation Dignity against Islamist militant groups and other opponents in eastern Libya, including Benghazi. Two months later, a separate campaign known as Libya Dawn emerged in western Libya, as Misrata-based armed groups and their allies fought rival factions, particularly over control of Tripoli International Airport.The fighting left Libya divided between rival political and military camps in the east and west, each establishing its own institutions and command structures.The security vacuum also allowed Islamic State (ISIS) to expand its presence. The group established a foothold in Derna before consolidating control over Sirte in 2015, turning Gaddafi's hometown into its main stronghold in Libya.ISIS imposed its rule through public executions, kidnappings and intimidation, while recruiting local fighters and former regime personnel.The United Nations Security Council warned in 2015 that the group's growing presence, alongside other extremist organisations, posed a serious threat to Libya and the wider region.In December 2015, a UN-brokered political agreement paved the way for the Government of National Accord, intended to reunify Libya's institutions. But the arrangement struggled to establish authority across the country. However, forces aligned with the internationally recognised government, supported by US air strikes, drove ISIS from Sirte in December 2016.Haftar's forces eventually launched an offensive against Tripoli in April 2019. The United Arab Emirates and Egypt supported Haftar's eastern camp, while Turkey provided crucial military support to Tripoli-aligned forces. Russia also backed Haftar's forces, including through personnel linked to the Wagner Group. These competing external interests reinforced Libya's internal divisions and complicated efforts to reach a political settlement.A UN-backed ceasefire in October 2020 halted large-scale fighting between the principal camps, but rival administrations and competing security structures endured.Libya after 2020The ceasefire of October 2020 ended large-scale fighting between Libya's rival eastern and western camps, but failed to reunify the country's political and military institutions.A UN-backed process installed Abdul Hamid Dbeibah as head of the Government of National Unity (GNU) in 2021, with elections intended to end the transitional period. The vote was postponed indefinitely amid disputes over electoral laws and candidate eligibility.In 2022, the eastern-based House of Representatives appointed a rival administration, leaving Libya divided between competing governments.The division remains central to Libya's current political and military landscape.The GNU, led by Dbeibah, operates from Tripoli in the west, while an eastern-based administration led by Osama Hamad is backed by the House of Representatives and Khalifa Haftar's Libyan Arab Armed Forces, also known as the Libyan National Army.Haftar's forces control much of eastern Libya and have expanded their influence and security presence in parts of the south.Western Libya, meanwhile, remains divided among government-aligned and other armed formations.Although the main east-west front has remained largely quiet since the ceasefire, rival military structures and local militia rivalries continue to pose security risks.The US Congressional Research Service reported in July 2026 that Haftar's forces had expanded their influence in the south and strengthened their military capabilities, including through drones.The political deadlock has also complicated efforts to organise national elections.In August 2026, a UN-facilitated agreement set out steps to reform the High National Elections Commission and address outstanding issues in the legal framework for presidential and parliamentary elections. The parties committed to work towards holding the vote within 24 months, rather than agreeing on a fixed election date.However, the process has encountered fresh resistance.In an October 14 briefing to the UN Security Council, UN Special Representative Hanna S. Tetteh said the House of Representatives had endorsed the agreement, but the High State Council rejected it on October 5, citing concerns over constitutional, legal and consensual procedures.The setback underlines how even a negotiated roadmap can become another point of contention between rival institutions.Oil wealth, economic pressure and failing public servicesDespite possessing Africa's largest proven oil reserves, Libya continues to face serious economic and fiscal vulnerabilities. Oil remains the backbone of its economy, accounting for 65 per cent of GDP, 93 per cent of exports and 72 per cent of government revenue in 2024, according to the World Bank.Production recovery has supported economic growth, but dependence on hydrocarbons leaves public finances exposed to disruptions caused by political disputes, fluctuating oil output and weak fiscal management.The International Monetary Fund warned in April 2026 that Libya's fiscal position had become increasingly vulnerable, estimating the budget deficit at around 30 per cent of GDP in 2025 and public debt at 146 per cent of GDP over the preceding two years. The IMF called for urgent fiscal adjustment to ease pressure on foreign exchange reserves, the dinar and inflation.In April, representatives of Libya's House of Representatives and High Council of State agreed to a unified national budget worth 190 billion Libyan dinars, or about $29.95 billion. It was the first such agreement since 2013.Central Bank Governor Naji Issa, who supervised the signing, described it as “a clear declaration that Libya is capable of overcoming its differences when a unified vision for its future is forged”.The agreement was intended to improve financial coordination and support development spending across the country, although its implementation remains a separate test. The deal marked progress in financial coordination, but it did not resolve the political divisions underpinning the country's wider crisis.The consequences of fragmentation are particularly visible in public services and infrastructure. The September 2023 floods that devastated Derna exposed failures in infrastructure maintenance, disaster preparedness and public accountability.Public services remain weak despite the country's oil wealth. The World Bank has highlighted shortcomings in healthcare, education, water and electricity provision, alongside high unemployment, corruption concerns and an underdeveloped private sector.These problems continue to constrain Libya's development, even as oil revenues offer the country significant financial resources.Fragile peace, uncertain futureAlthough Libya has avoided a return to full-scale civil war since the 2020 ceasefire, rival military structures, powerful armed groups and foreign involvement continue to threaten stability.Briefing the UN Security Council on October 14, Tetteh warned that “institutional and political fragmentation have continued to impact negatively on the economic and security situation in the country”.She said many Libyans were seeing their purchasing power eroded by rising food prices, a weaker dinar and inflation above 14 per cent, while access to essential public services remained unreliable.Tetteh also cautioned that the path to stability remained difficult, saying, “The path to a stable, unified, and prosperous Libya remains long, but our destination remains within reach.” She urged Libyan political actors to demonstrate the flexibility and political will needed to reach common ground.Fifteen years after Gaddafi's death, Libya's challenge is no longer simply to prevent another civil war. It is to build a state capable of controlling armed groups, managing oil revenues transparently and delivering reliable public services.The election roadmap and unified budget offer potential steps towards greater stability, but neither guarantees lasting peace. Libya's future will depend on whether rival leaders can turn these commitments into a functioning political settlement.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Another tiger captured near Gudalur in the Nilgiris
articles.summary: UDHAGAMANDALAM: A tiger that is suspected to have preyed on livestock in and around O-Valley near Gudalur in the Nilgiris in the past few weeks was on
articles.body: UDHAGAMANDALAM: A tiger that is suspected to have preyed on livestock in and around O-Valley near Gudalur in the Nilgiris in the past few weeks was on Thursday found trapped in a cage set up by the forest department. The tiger, aged around 13 years, was trapped a month after another tiger, which is suspected to have killed two men, had been trapped in the same area by the forest department.Forest department personnel tied a goat inside the cage to lure the tiger that killed livestock. The tiger was found lying inside the cage in a semi-conscious state on Thursday morning. A forest department staff member wearing protective gear approached the animal, but it remained in the same condition. The tiger was subsequently shifted to a smaller cage for transportation.Gudalur forest range officer P Devaraj said the big cat was caught in their camera traps a couple of times in the last few weeks. “Deep wounds were found on its face. The animal looked very tired. Generally, wounds caused by infighting would heal. But this 13-year-old tiger was found to be very tired. We are planning to shift it to Vandalur zoo in Chennai. Once an official order is issued, it will be moved,” he said.On Sept 18, the forest department trapped a tiger that is suspected to have killed two men. The animal was captured following a 29-day search operation. articles.title: Govt nod to stipend hike for junior resident doctors, DNB trainees
articles.summary: Jharkhand govt approves stipend hike for junior resident doctors in govt medical colleges; proposal initiated to revise DNB trainee stipends at RINPAS.
articles.body: Ranchi: In a move aimed at boosting doctors’ morale and strengthening healthcare services, the state health department on Thursday announced an increase in the monthly stipend of junior resident (academic) doctors in govt medical colleges and hospitals, while also initiating action to revise stipends for DNB trainees at the Ranchi Institute of Neuro-Psychiatry and Allied Sciences (RINPAS), Kanke.Under a govt resolution dated April 27, 2026, the stipend for first-year junior residents has been raised from Rs 54,500 to Rs 70,000 per month, for second-year residents from Rs 58,500 to Rs 75,000, and for third-year residents from Rs 63,000 to Rs 80,000.The health department has also acted on a proposal to revise stipends for DNB trainees at RINPAS in line with prescribed norms. Under the proposed structure, broad speciality DNB trainees would receive a minimum stipend of Rs 43,000, Rs 45,000 and Rs 47,000 per month in the first, second and third years respectively. Post-diploma DNB trainees would be entitled to Rs 45,000 and Rs 47,000 per month during the first and second years of training.Health minister Irfan Ansari said, “The govt is committed to ensuring dignity and better working conditions for doctors as they are an integral part of our healthcare system.”The minister added that the govt’s priority was not only to increase stipends but also to improve healthcare infrastructure, provide modern equipment in hospitals and create better working conditions for medical professionals. “The revision would help attract and retain talented doctors in Jharkhand,” he said.Additional chief secretary, health, Ajoy Kumar Singh said the proposal had been approved following the minister’s directions. “The objective is to boost the morale of both junior and senior doctors and provide them with better working conditions. The govt has consistently taken steps to improve salaries and stipends of medical professionals,” he said.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: BJP national president’s 3 day state visit from today
articles.summary: BJP national president Nitin Nabin begins a 3-day Jharkhand visit, arriving in Ranchi Oct 23 to attend the BJP state executive committee meeting on Oct 24.
articles.body: Ranchi: State BJP is geared up to welcome its national president, Nitin Nabin, who will arrive in Ranchi on Friday on a three-day visit and attend the inaugural session of the party’s state executive committee meeting on Oct 24.The party has put up flags, banners and bunting across the capital, while state BJP president Aditya Sahu reviewed preparations with office-bearers on Thursday.State BJP general secretary Amar Kumar Bauri said, “Navin’s visit has generated enthusiasm among party workers across Jharkhand. He is scheduled to reach Ranchi airport at 7 pm on Oct 23, where BJP workers have planned a traditional welcome with tribal cultural performances, drums and floral showers.”During his visit, Nabin is expected to address party leaders and workers at the state executive committee meeting and outline the party’s organisational and political agenda ahead. Senior BJP leaders and office-bearers from across the state are expected to attend the programme.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Harish blames Congress for drought, crop losses on 12L acres across state
articles.summary: Harish Rao blames Telangana Congress govt for “drought-created” crop losses on 12 lakh acres, citing poor irrigation and power; seeks drought declaration and aid.
articles.body: Hyderabad: Former minister T Harish Rao alleged that Telangana is facing a “Congress-created drought” due to the state govt’s failure to ensure adequate irrigation and power supply, resulting in crops drying up on nearly 12 lakh acres across the state.He demanded that the state govt immediately declare drought-hit mandals, provide compensation for crop losses, release ₹12,000 in assistance to agricultural labourers, ensure 24-hour quality power supply, operate irrigation projects round the clock, and take measures to address drinking water shortages across the state.After visiting drought-hit paddy fields in Burugupalli village, Gajwel mandal, Siddipet district, on Thursday, Harish met with affected farmers. He reviewed crop losses due to a lack of water and electricity. He accused the Congress govt of ignoring repeated warnings from scientists and agricultural experts about possible drought conditions due to El Nino and of failing to take preventive measures in time.Addressing reporters, Harish said farmers in several districts, including Adilabad, Karimnagar, Nalgonda, Medak, Khammam and Mahabubnagar, had suffered severe crop losses. He alleged that the state govt had neither secured sufficient coal stocks nor purchased adequate power in advance, leading to an electricity shortage during the critical crop season. Instead of accepting responsibility, he said, the govt was attempting to blame officials for the crisis.The BRS leader also accused the Congress govt of not operating lift irrigation schemes such as Kannepalli, Devadula and Kalwakurthy at full capacity, resulting in irrigation shortages and widespread crop damage. He claimed that hundreds of acres in the Gajwel region alone had dried up just as crops were nearing harvest.Citing individual cases, Harish said several farmers had spent thousands of rupees on diesel generators to save their crops but still suffered heavy losses because of irregular power supply and low-voltage issues.Drawing comparisons with the previous BRS govt, he said uninterrupted power and irrigation facilities had helped farmers achieve record agricultural production even during difficult periods.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news.
